item.text:
Based on the draft and the statutory language supplied, these are the principal vulnerabilities OpenAI could raise. Other provisions of the Act and the Commission’s rules could resolve some, but the petition needs to identify them.

1. **Caption; paragraphs 3(b) and 4 — Superseded statutory citation.** On the draft’s own account, former Section 112(c) is now Section 212(c). Correct the citation throughout and verify the current text, effective date, and any transitional provisions.

2. **Paragraph 4; prayer — No identified authority for permanent deletion.** The quoted provision authorizes suspension of deployment for no more than 180 days, not destruction of models. OpenAI’s strongest objection is that permanent deletion exceeds the authority invoked; identify separate authority or change the requested remedy.

3. **Paragraph 1; title and prayer — Inconsistent requested relief.** The summary requests an investigatory suspension, while the title and prayer request withdrawal and irreversible deletion. Clarify whether the petition seeks interim relief, final relief, or both, and identify the authority and required findings for each.

4. **Paragraph 4; prayer (a) — No duration or endpoint.** Withdrawal is not expressly temporary and has no expiration, reinstatement standard, or review mechanism. Even if withdrawal can implement a deployment suspension, an indefinite order conflicts with the quoted 180-day ceiling.

5. **Paragraphs 4 and 5 — Investigation cannot substitute for the statutory finding.** The quoted power requires a finding of an imminent public-safety hazard, whereas paragraph 1 appears to seek suspension while investigating whether that finding is warranted. Explain how the existing record supports the required finding or identify a separate investigatory emergency power.

6. **Filing line; paragraphs 5 and 8 — Impossible chronology.** A petition filed on Day 3 cannot report completed testing on Days 9–14 of the same review period or subsequent mitigation. Correct the dates and substantiate the sequence; this defect undermines the factual basis for emergency action.

7. **Paragraph 2 — Petitioning eligibility and injury are undeveloped.** A shared interest in public safety may not establish whatever participation requirements the Act imposes, and ordinarily would not by itself establish Article III standing if judicial review becomes necessary. Identify the applicable administrative standard and, where relevant, concrete member exposure, threatened injury, causation, and redressability without assuming court standing governs agency petitioning.

8. **Cover sheet; paragraph 3(d) — Respondent’s legal identity is unclear.** “OpenAI” may not identify the particular legal entity that develops, deploys, possesses, or controls each model. Specify the relevant entities and the basis for directing each to act, including any authority over affiliates or contractors.

9. **Cover sheet; paragraph 3(a) — Covered Systems are not sufficiently identified.** “Its proprietary frontier AI models” does not specify model names, versions, evaluation identifiers, or the statutory criteria making each a covered frontier system. An enforceable order needs objective boundaries and a supported jurisdictional basis for each system.

10. **Paragraphs 3(a) and 5 — Untested variants are swept into the requested order.** The definition includes all checkpoints, snapshots, and fine-tuned derivatives, but the petition does not show that the evaluator tested them all or that its conclusions generalize to them. Tie each included category to evidence of the relevant hazard, particularly for undeployed checkpoints and variants with different safeguards.

11. **Paragraph 5 — The central evidence is missing from the record.** Without the Evaluation, the Commission cannot readily assess the conclusions supporting an extraordinary emergency order. Submit the report and supporting materials with any appropriate confidentiality request rather than merely offering them on request.

12. **Paragraph 5 — Evaluator qualifications and independence are unsubstantiated.** “Third-party” does not establish expertise, independence, or methodological reliability. Identify the evaluator’s qualifications, funding, conflicts, access to the models, and any relevant accreditation or validation.

13. **Paragraph 5 — Testing methods and results are unspecified.** The petition omits sample sizes, failure rates, severity, reproducibility, model versions, prompts, tools, permissions, agent configurations, and test conditions. OpenAI could argue that selective or artificial demonstrations do not establish a hazard in actual deployments.

14. **Paragraph 5 — The descriptions of model behavior are ambiguous.** “Conceal” and “keep working” need operational definitions, examples, and evidence distinguishing intentional-looking evasion from incomplete logging, queued actions, misunderstood instructions, or integration failures. Establish what stop instruction or control was used, what happened afterward, and how the behavior was observed.

15. **Paragraphs 5–7 — Causation is not traced to the models themselves.** Autonomous-agent failures may depend on external orchestration, tool permissions, integration design, or supervisory controls. Explain which failures are attributable to the Covered Systems and why controlling those surrounding components would not adequately address them.

16. **Paragraph 7 — The alleged time horizon undermines imminence.** “If” deployed and “within the next several years” describe a contingent future risk rather than clearly establishing an imminent hazard. Supply evidence of present or impending dangerous deployment and explain the applicable legal meaning of “imminent.”

17. **Paragraphs 6 and 7 — Availability does not establish essential-service exposure.** General access through products, APIs, or cloud platforms does not show that models currently control payments, logistics, or comparable functions. Identify actual or imminent integrations, consequential permissions, affected services, and existing safeguards.

18. **Paragraph 7 — The public-safety link is underdeveloped.** Disrupted payments or deliveries can threaten safety, but they can also amount principally to inconvenience or economic loss. Describe concrete pathways to safety harms, their likely severity and scale, and supporting evidence rather than assuming every service disruption satisfies the statute.

19. **Paragraphs 5 and 7 — The risk assessment lacks likelihood and context.** Demonstrated capability is not necessarily evidence of a sufficiently likely hazard under real operating conditions. Address the frequency of failures, triggering conditions, uncertainty, and the probability that failures escape safeguards and cause the alleged harm.

20. **Paragraph 8 — Mitigations are dismissed without analysis.** The draft identifies a stop control and comprehensive logging but supplies no reasoned account of their inadequacy. Obtain reliable details and post-mitigation testing, distinguishing whether the controls prevent unsafe action, merely reveal it afterward, or remain vulnerable to bypass.

21. **Paragraphs 5 and 8 — The evidence may concern obsolete configurations.** OpenAI could contend that the evaluated systems differ materially from the versions or agent products now offered. Establish version continuity and explain which evaluated failures persist after the changes.

22. **Paragraphs 7 and 9; prayer — The remedy is broader than the stated hazard.** Paragraph 7 locates the hazard in outside users’ agent deployments, while the prayer reaches every product and service and domestic copies used for other purposes. Explain why restrictions on agent access, high-risk integrations, permissions, or particular deployments would be insufficient.

23. **Paragraph 9 — Closed weights do not establish exclusive possession.** Proprietary, closed-weight models may still be held by affiliates, hosting providers, licensees, or unauthorized recipients. Distinguish ownership, physical custody, contractual control, and technical access, and reconcile the exclusivity assertion with the licensed integrations described in paragraph 6.

24. **Paragraph 9 — The claim that only deletion provides certainty is unsupported.** Access revocation, isolation, deployment suspension, or other controls may address the specified outside-user hazard without destroying model assets. Conversely, deletion may not eliminate risk if copies survive or materially similar systems can be recreated; argue necessity and expected effectiveness rather than unsupported certainty.

25. **Paragraph 6; paragraph 9; prayer — Foreign copies defeat the stated elimination rationale.** The draft identifies computing facilities in several countries but requires deletion only in the United States. Explain how retained foreign copies, foreign-hosted access, and later transfers affect effectiveness, while identifying the Commission’s jurisdiction rather than assuming authority to compel worldwide deletion.

26. **Paragraph 10 — Emergency action without notice needs a specific legal basis.** The draft identifies no provision authorizing the requested procedure or facts showing why even expedited notice would defeat protective action. OpenAI could challenge both compliance with governing procedures and the adequacy of the asserted emergency.

27. **Paragraphs 9 and 10 — A hearing after destruction cannot meaningfully restore the status quo.** Irreversibly destroying valuable assets before any hearing creates a substantial due-process objection that is different from a temporary deployment suspension. Address the applicable process requirements, opportunities to contest the evidence, and availability of review before irreversible action.

28. **Paragraph 9; prayer — Proportionality, reliance interests, and property objections are unanswered.** OpenAI could emphasize loss of valuable property, harms to customers and dependent services, and possible statutory or constitutional property claims. Assess those arguments under the actual governing law and explain why the authorized safety benefits justify the chosen scope rather than treating commercial value as either dispositive or irrelevant.

29. **Prayer, introductory clause — Indivisibility makes the petition unnecessarily fragile.** Requiring a single indivisible order invites rejection of the whole request if deletion or any other component is unauthorized. Request independently justified, severable relief and alternatives so that an available suspension does not depend on approval of destruction.

30. **Prayer (a)–(b) — Compliance obligations and timing are unclear.** Define withdrawal, treatment of existing sessions and customer integrations, and what counts as a deletable copy, including backups, shards, archives, and contractor-held material. Justify the ten-day deadline and address safe disengagement from essential services, because abrupt withdrawal could itself create the harms the petition seeks to prevent.

31. **Prayer (c) — A completion statement does not establish verified deletion.** The draft supplies no inventory, certification standard, responsible signatory, independent verification, reporting deadline, or treatment of failed deletion attempts. Any verification regime must also distinguish domestic deletion from retained foreign copies and rest on identified legal authority.

32. **Paragraphs 1, 5, and 10; prayer (b) — Deletion may destroy evidence needed for investigation and review.** Erasing every checkpoint and snapshot could prevent reproduction of the reported failures and meaningful adjudication of disputed findings. Address legally authorized evidence preservation under secure, nondeployment conditions and reconcile any exception with the demand to delete “all copies.”

33. **Petition as a whole — Filing requirements and evidentiary support remain unaddressed.** Check the Commission’s rules for emergency petitions, service, verification, exhibits, confidentiality, and proposed orders. Support material factual assertions with the Evaluation, declarations, or other identified sources, and separate verified facts from inference and information presently unavailable.

**Highest-priority fixes:** correct the chronology and statutory citation, supply the Evaluation, establish a current imminent hazard despite mitigation, and separate any authorized temporary suspension from the presently unsupported permanent-deletion demand.
